title: Risk culture, decision bias and the use of data
blurb: Recognize the four decision biases named in PRINCE2 7, explain why risk culture matters, and describe how data supports risk management.
question: A board keeps approving plans because 'our projects always come good', and dismisses warnings about the supplier. Which decision bias is this?

teach.body: PRINCE2 7 adds guidance on risk culture: the shared attitudes and behaviours that decide whether people actually raise, discuss and act on risks. In plain English: the best risk register is useless if people hide bad news or nobody dares to challenge the boss. A healthy culture makes it normal to raise threats and opportunities early and to question assumptions.

Formally: decision bias is natural and largely positive, because it lets the brain make rapid decisions every day. Sometimes, though, it leads to less effective decisions about risk. In plain English: mental shortcuts usually help us, but on a project they can make us underrate threats, overrate near-term worries or stay quiet to keep the peace. Knowing the named biases helps teams spot them.

teach.body: PRINCE2 7 encourages using data and analytics to identify and assess risks: for example, past project data to estimate probability, automated monitoring of early warning indicators, and predictive forecasting of exposure. Evidence helps counter bias, because decisions rest on what the data shows rather than on gut feeling alone. Data should be presented in the form stakeholders prefer.

teach.h: Worked scenario: a regional airport baggage system
teach.body: At Kestrel Regional Airport, project manager Daniel Fraser notices the team keeps agreeing with the operations director in risk workshops, and nobody mentions the baggage supplier's poor record (groupthink). The board also assumes testing will pass first time (optimism bias). Daniel asks each person to write risks down privately before discussion, and uses data from the last three system upgrades to show that first-time test passes happened only once.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Optimism bias DISCOUNTS disadvantageous risk; loss aversion OVERWEIGHTS avoiding loss. (2) Groupthink values group cohesion over voicing a different view. (3) 'Proximity' as a bias (near things feel riskier) is not risk proximity (how near in time a risk may occur). (4) Bias is natural and mostly useful; the aim is awareness, not elimination.

items: Risk culture affects whether risks are raised, discussed and acted on.
Decision bias is natural and largely positive but can harm risk decisions.
Loss aversion: avoiding loss valued over making a gain.
Optimism bias: discounting disadvantageous risk, assuming success. Groupthink: cohesion over dissent.
Proximity bias: near-term situations seen as riskier. Data and analytics help identify and assess risks.

summary: You can now recognize loss aversion, optimism bias, groupthink and proximity bias, and explain why decision bias is natural but can weaken risk decisions. You can also describe how a healthy risk culture and the use of data improve risk management.

A.q: Which decision bias describes a mindset that values avoiding a loss more than making a gain?
A.why: Loss aversion is a mindset that values the avoidance of loss over making a gain (manual 9.2.4).

whyNot.0: Optimism bias discounts disadvantageous risk on the assumption things will go well.
whyNot.1: Groupthink values group cohesion over voicing a different view.
whyNot.3: Proximity bias sees near-term situations as riskier and more important.

A.q: Which statement about decision bias is correct?
options: It is natural and largely positive but can lead to poorer decisions
It is a sign of poor management and must be removed from the team
It affects the project board but not the people doing the work
It is recorded as a risk cause in the risk management approach
A.why: Decision bias is natural and largely positive, letting people decide quickly, but it can sometimes result in less effective decisions.

whyNot.1: Bias is natural; the aim is to recognize it, not treat it as poor management.
whyNot.2: Bias can affect anyone involved in risk decisions.
whyNot.3: The approach describes procedures; it does not record specific causes.

A.q: What does PRINCE2 7 say data and analytics can be used for in the risk practice?
options: To set the business's risk appetite
A.why: Use of data (9.3.2.6) applies data and analytics to help identify and assess risks.

whyNot.0: Risk appetite is set by the business, not derived by analytics.
whyNot.2: Data supports the register; the register remains the record of risks.
whyNot.3: Owners are agreed in the implement step, not appointed by analytics.

B.q: A project team never challenges the sponsor's estimates in meetings because they want to keep a good atmosphere. Which bias is this?
B.why: Valuing group cohesion over expressing an alternative view is groupthink.

whyNot.0: Loss aversion is about avoiding losses rather than making gains.
whyNot.1: Proximity bias concerns near-term situations feeling riskier.
whyNot.2: Optimism bias is assuming success, not staying quiet to keep harmony.

B.q: A board spends every meeting on this month's minor supplier delay and does not discuss a large regulatory threat expected next year. Which bias is most likely at work?
B.why: Proximity bias makes situations closer in time seem riskier and more important than those further in the future.

whyNot.1: Nothing suggests members are suppressing dissent to keep the peace.
whyNot.2: The pattern is about timing, not valuing avoidance of loss over gain.
whyNot.3: The board is not assuming success; it is focusing on near-term matters.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Optimism bias discounts disadvantageous risk.
2. Groupthink encourages people to voice alternative views.
3. Proximity bias treats near-term situations as more important.
4. Loss aversion values making a gain over avoiding a loss.
B.why: Optimism bias discounts disadvantageous risk (1); proximity bias sees near-term situations as riskier and more important (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: groupthink suppresses alternative views.
whyNot.1: Both are false: groupthink suppresses dissent, and loss aversion favours avoiding loss.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: loss aversion values avoiding a loss over making a gain.

C.q: A team rates every threat as 'low' because 'we delivered the last project on time'. Which bias is this, and what would best counter it?
options: Loss aversion; rely on the most senior person's view
Optimism bias; base estimates on data from past projects
Groupthink; record each threat in the daily log
Proximity; review threats at the next stage boundary
C.why: Assuming success and discounting threats is optimism bias; evidence from data helps counter it.

whyNot.0: This is not about valuing loss avoidance, and deferring to seniority can add bias.
whyNot.2: No group pressure is described, and the daily log does not address bias.
whyNot.3: Timing is not the issue; the team is assuming things will go well.

C.q: A board turns down a low-cost opportunity with a likely large gain because a small part of the budget could be lost. Which bias is this, and which kind of risk is being under-valued?
C.why: Valuing avoiding a loss over making a gain is loss aversion, and here it leads the board to under-value an opportunity.

whyNot.1: Optimism bias discounts threats on the assumption of success; here the board is overly cautious about a loss.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests the group is suppressing dissent.
whyNot.3: The decision is not driven by how near in time things are.

C.q: Which statement best links risk culture and the use of data?
options: Data removes the need for people to raise risks themselves
Culture is set in the risk register and data in the approach
Evidence from data helps challenge biased views in an open culture
Data is used by the business layer to set the project's tolerance
C.why: An open risk culture lets people raise and challenge views; data and analytics provide evidence to identify and assess risks, which helps counter bias.

whyNot.0: Data supports people; it does not replace them raising risks.
whyNot.1: Neither culture nor data is defined by where it is recorded.
whyNot.3: The project board sets risk tolerance, based on the business's risk appetite.

reteach.title: Planning a holiday with friends
reteach.question: Which bias is behind 'it never rains in May', and which behind 'nobody wanted to argue with Sam about the date'?

blocks.body: 'It never rains in May' assumes success and discounts a threat: optimism bias. Nobody arguing with Sam to keep the peace is groupthink. Refusing a cheap upgrade in case you lose the deposit is loss aversion. Worrying about this week's packing and forgetting to renew passports for next month is proximity bias. Checking last year's weather data is the use of data.

blocks.text: Bias is normal: the point is to notice it, not to pretend it away.

explain.body: Discounting disadvantageous risk on the assumption that things will be successful.

test.q: Which bias assumes things are likely to go well and so discounts threats?
test.why: Optimism bias discounts disadvantageous risk on the assumption of success.

explain.body: Valuing social cohesion in a group more than voicing a different view or reaching the right decision.

options: Valuing avoiding a loss over a gain
test.why: Groupthink values social cohesion more than expressing an alternative view.

explain.body: Situations closer in time are seen as riskier and more important than those in the future.

test.q: In decision bias, what does 'proximity' mean?
options: Nearer situations seem riskier and more important
The estimated time before a particular risk might occur
How quickly a risk would affect objectives
Risks raised by people close to the sponsor
test.why: As a bias, proximity is a mindset where nearer situations are seen as riskier and more important.

whyNot.1: That is risk proximity, a measure, not the bias.
whyNot.3: This is not a PRINCE2 meaning of proximity.

explain.body: Data and analytics help identify and assess risks, giving evidence that tempers bias.

test.q: How does the use of data support the risk practice?
options: It sets the risk budget for each stage
It replaces the project board's judgement
It helps identify and assess risks
It decides who owns each risk
test.why: Data and analytics are used to identify and assess risks.

whyNot.0: Budgets are set in planning, not by data on its own.
whyNot.1: Data informs the board; it does not replace its decisions.
whyNot.3: Ownership is agreed in the implement step.
